source_excerpt: It’s important to not freeze the minion wave too close or under your tower as it can get you killed. During the laning phase, having it under your tower may allow the enemy Jungler to dive you. It will also not freeze here.

tip: Freezing is harder early against champions with fast wave clear, since they can poke or fight you while you try to hold the wave — it's often safer to attempt after your first back once you have items.
rationale: Extra damage and defensive items from your first back give you the survivability to hold a freeze against a strong-clearing opponent.
source_excerpt: Freezing is not the easiest thing to do in the early game if you’re against champions who can quickly clear waves. This is because they may be able to poke you and fight you if you try to freeze. Freezing (in some cases) is best done after your first back when you have items and damage to protect yourself with.

tip: As Camille, keep the wave close to your own tower but outside its range, so you can bounce your Hookshot off a wall onto a mispositioned Gnar.
rationale: Camille needs the wave near her tower to convert her E's engage range into a safe follow-up on Gnar.
source_excerpt: Camille would like the wave to be close to her tower so she can use her Hookshot (E) on a wall and then bounce onto Gnar to deal damage to him.

tip: As Gnar, keep the wave near your own tower so Camille can't dive you if she engages, since you have no reliable way to punish her overextension otherwise.
rationale: Denying Camille the dive-friendly wave state removes her main way of abusing the matchup early.
source_excerpt: Having the wave near the tower will prevent Camille from being able to play aggressive and kill the Gnar because she will not be able to dive him early.

tip: As Darius, avoid using your Q to push the wave unless you can land it on the enemy champion, since it can shove the lane out of the position you want.
rationale: Pushing the wave with Q trades away Darius's ability to keep the lane in the aggressive, close-range state his kit needs.
source_excerpt: Darius needs to be very careful when it comes to using his abilities. His Q has an AOE indicator that can push waves. He wants to avoid using this ability unless he can get on the enemy.

tip: As Teemo, keep the wave close to your own tower until level 6, then start pushing and using Shrooms to take the first tower.
rationale: Teemo's Blind and stronger trading power come online at 6, at which point pushing to threaten the first tower becomes viable.
source_excerpt: At level 6, Teemo wants to start pushing and abusing his kit to the maximum. By placing shrooms around the lane, he can constantly get the wave pushing and take the First Tower.

tip: As Renekton, keep the wave even and near the middle of the lane so you can all-in the enemy whenever you gain a level or item advantage.
rationale: Pushing the enemy to their own tower lets them freeze and denies Renekton the ability to engage on his advantage.
source_excerpt: If Renekton pushes the enemy to their tower and the enemy freezes, he will be unable to engage on the enemy and push his advantage in lane.

tip: As Maokai, keep the wave on your own side of the lane, since pushing lets Renekton use his E on the minions to close the gap and engage on you.
rationale: Maokai's lack of mobility means he needs to deny Renekton the wave state that enables an easy engage.
source_excerpt: If Maokai pushes the wave, Renekton, just by using his E on the minions, will be able to get incredibly close and engage on him and may even be able to kill him.

tip: As Twisted Fate, keep the wave near your own tower so Zed can't use his kit or early damage to poke you down.
rationale: Zed is one of Twisted Fate's hardest matchups, so removing his engage angle onto the wave is a priority.
source_excerpt: If Twisted Fate has the wave near his tower, Zed will be unable to utilize his kit or early game damage. This is a good thing as it will prevent Zed from using his abilities to poke Twisted Fate down.

tip: As Zed, avoid pushing the wave under Twisted Fate's tower, since the tower prevents you from engaging or fighting him there, including at his level 3 all-in window.
rationale: Zed's burst-reliant playstyle needs the wave in a neutral or favorable spot to actually reach Twisted Fate.
source_excerpt: If Zed pushes the lane under Twisted Fates tower, he would be unable to engage or fight him because of the tower.

tip: As Kog'Maw and Lulu against Twitch and Janna, keep the wave even in the middle of the lane so you can use your poke and chase potential while you scale, without getting pushed under your own tower.
rationale: This duo needs time to scale, so avoiding a losing wave state that exposes them to ganks or lost tower is essential.
source_excerpt: These two champions need to scale, they must not get put behind nor pushed under their tower and lose it. This means they need to keep it out of range of their tower and in a position where they can be aggressive- like in the middle of the lane.

tip: As Twitch and Janna, keep the wave closer to your own side or the middle rather than overextending, since Twitch is squishy early and Janna can't save him if the jungler ganks.
rationale: This lane lacks the early tools to punish an overextension if it's caught, so wave position has to compensate.
source_excerpt: They do not want to overextend as they might get surprise ganks from the enemy Jungler. While Janna can keep her ADC alive, Twitch is rather squishy in the early game with no real way of protecting himself.

tip: As Miss Fortune and Zyra, use your early damage and poke advantage to freeze the wave near your own tower and zone the enemy off CS.
rationale: This duo's early poke lead converts directly into a zone-and-deny freeze against squishier opponents.
source_excerpt: Because Miss Fortune and Zyra have insane damage and poke in the early game, they are able to zone and deny the enemy CS by freezing near their own tower.

tip: As Seraphine and Soraka, keep the wave even and in the middle of the lane rather than overpushing, so you aren't zoned off farm while you scale up.
rationale: This duo lacks early damage, so avoiding a wave state the enemy can punish is more important than being aggressive.
source_excerpt: One way of preventing them doing this is by keeping the wave outside of your tower range and ideally in the middle of the lane. Seraphine needs time to scale, so she must be able to get as much farm as possible.

tip: As Caitlyn and Morgana, push the wave relentlessly and maintain strong ward coverage, since your range, poke, and wave clear let you keep the enemy under constant pressure.
rationale: A duo with a clear damage and clear-speed edge should convert it into sustained pushes rather than passive play, while warding to avoid the jungler punishing the overextension.
source_excerpt: This bot lane duo can quickly push and keep it pushed thanks to their abilities and overall early-game damage. They have great wave clear and should be no match for the enemy. Because they will be pushing frequently, they need to make sure that they have sufficient ward coverage around the lane to spot the enemy Jungler.

tip: As Kog'Maw and Lulu against Caitlyn and Morgana, keep the wave close to your own tower but outside its range and avoid pushing at all costs, so you aren't denied farm or zoned while you scale.
rationale: Against a lane with a clear early advantage, this duo has to prioritize safety over CS efficiency to survive to their scaling window.
source_excerpt: It’s important to keep it close and outside of tower range to prevent losing first tower while also being able to farm and not get denied or zoned by Morgana or Caitlyn. Avoid pushing at all costs and don’t let them push you into tower.

tip: If you're ahead and freezing, position yourself in front of the wave to threaten and deny the enemy's farm, but check the map first in case they're baiting a skirmish.
rationale: Standing in the wave to zone works only if it isn't walking you into a setup, so a map check has to precede the play.
source_excerpt: If you’re ahead of the enemy and you’re freezing, you can position yourself in front of the minion wave to deny the enemy farm and gold. If they overextend in attempts to get the farm, you will be able to engage on them. Make sure you check the map before you engage on them though because they may be baiting you into a 1v2 skirmish.

tip: If the enemy is trying to reset the wave, intercept it before it reaches your tower, thin it down while tanking, then drop aggro when your reinforcements arrive to create a freeze.
rationale: Meeting the enemy's push away from your tower converts what would have been a reset into a favorable freeze for you instead.
source_excerpt: If the enemy is trying to make the wave reset, you can meet it before it hits your tower and thin it down while taking it and then dropping aggro when your minions arrive. This will create a freeze and will allow you to deny.

tip: Be extra cautious trying to freeze a cannon wave, since it's much less predictable and can easily push against you instead of holding.
rationale: The cannon minion's extra health and damage make the usual freeze math unreliable.
source_excerpt: Cannon minions are jerks. They’re very trolly in lane and it feels like their sole purpose is to mess up your wave management! Freezing on a cannon wave is 50/50 and it can work in your favor, but also against you.

tip: To break an enemy's freeze on your own, clear the minions and shove the wave into the enemy's tower so it resets or bounces into a more favorable position.
rationale: Forcing the wave into their tower removes the local minion advantage the enemy is using to hold the freeze against you.
source_excerpt: In order for you to break the freeze on your own, you need to clear the minions and shove it into the enemies tower. This will make the tower reset or bounce the wave and let it end up in a much more favorable position.

tip: Prefer breaking a freeze yourself over calling your jungler for help, since pulling them in can cost your team map pressure and put other lanes behind.
rationale: Solving the problem locally avoids exporting the cost of a bad freeze onto the rest of your team.
source_excerpt: The first option is much more viable than the second because it doesn’t require assistance. If your Jungler comes to help, your team might be losing pressure around the map and this could put your Jungler and other lanes behind.

tip: To slow push a wave, kill only the caster minions in it, letting the melee minions (which take longer to die) build a numbers advantage that pushes the wave toward the enemy over time.
rationale: Removing the fast-dying casters while leaving the tankier melee minions is what produces the gradual, growing push.
source_excerpt: To slow push a wave, all you need to do is kill the caster minions in the enemies wave. You can do this with your basic attacks as well as using your abilities to take them down faster.

tip: Use a slow push to draw the enemy's attention to a growing wave while you take an objective or move elsewhere on the map, since an unanswered slow push can take down multiple towers on its own.
rationale: A slow push forces a response from the enemy, and if it doesn't get one it becomes a second, self-sufficient threat.
source_excerpt: You should slow push a minion wave so it can draw the enemies attention which will allow you to take an objective or be somewhere else on the map. A slow-pushed wave can take down multiple towers if done correctly and if it is left unattended by the enemy.

tip: Avoid slow pushing during the early laning phase, since it can cost you CS and gold and put you in bad trades — save it for the later stages of laning and beyond.
rationale: Slow pushing sacrifices short-term farming efficiency for a payoff that only matters once you're ready to leave lane.
source_excerpt: Generally, you want to avoid using slow pushing in the laning phase (the early stages) because it will mess up your laning and it can make you miss out on CS and gold.

tip: Before roaming to help another lane, set up a slow push first so your tower isn't left exposed to a fast-pushing enemy wave while you're away.
rationale: Leaving a neutral or frozen wave means the enemy is free to push your tower unchallenged during your roam.
source_excerpt: Before you go to help other laners, you need to have the lane slow pushing. This is a must do before leaving your lane as it will stop the enemy from pushing quickly and taking down your tower while you’re missing.

tip: While roaming, frequently check back on your lane to see what the wave and the enemy are doing, and return promptly if the wave is being pushed back quickly.
rationale: A slow push left unattended for too long can be undone if you don't monitor and react to the enemy's response.
source_excerpt: While you’re gone, make sure to frequently check back at your lane to see what the minions are doing and where the enemy is. If they are pushing it back quickly, you will need to return to lane as soon as you can.

tip: In the mid and late game, slow push the wave before recalling so it grows into a big wave and starts pressuring the nearest objective while you're away picking up items.
rationale: A recall doesn't have to cost map pressure if the wave left behind is doing work on its own.
source_excerpt: In the mid and late game, if you want to Recall, you should slow push the wave in order for it to start forming a big wave which will eventually start applying pressure to the closest objective.

tip: During the early laning phase, fast push the wave before recalling rather than slow pushing it — slow pushing to back is a later-game technique.
rationale: Slow pushing takes time to build that isn't worth spending during the early laning phase, where a quick fast push serves the recall better.
source_excerpt: You only want to slow push to back if you’re in the later stages of the game and not in the early game, in this case, you want to fast push, not slow push.

tip: Before leaving your lane to contest an objective like Dragon, Rift Herald, or Baron, set up a slow push first so the enemy can't freely push and take your towers while you're occupied.
rationale: An unattended lane during an objective fight is a towers-for-objective trade you don't have to accept if the wave is already working for you.
source_excerpt: If you do not slow push the wave before leaving to take the objective, the enemy may push the lane and start taking your towers while you’re busy being occupied.

tip: When the enemy is forced to clear a big slow-pushed wave at their tower, use that window to pressure and take an objective elsewhere, since it effectively creates a 4v5 for them.
rationale: An enemy occupied clearing a wave is a player missing from a fight or objective contest elsewhere on the map.
source_excerpt: During this time, your team could pressure the objective and try to take it why the enemy goes to clear the wave. A good time to do this is as soon as it starts attacking the tower. Fighting like this will make any fight 4v5 as an enemy will be missing trying to clear the tower.

tip: To fast push a wave, kill the melee (front) minions and any cannon minions first using autos and AOE abilities, since more minions relative to the enemy makes the push faster and stronger.
rationale: Melee minions block the wave's advance the longest, so clearing them first is what actually speeds the push.
source_excerpt: To fast push a wave you need to kill all the melee minions (the front minions) as quickly as you can as well as any cannon minions in the lane. You should use your auto attacks as well as your AOE abilities to make the wave clearing quicker.

tip: When setting up to dive the enemy under their own tower, build up a bigger minion wave first so it helps tank tower shots and adds extra damage onto the enemy.
rationale: A larger wave both soaks tower aggro and contributes damage, making an otherwise risky dive far safer.
source_excerpt: When you want to dive the enemy, you should have as many minions around you as possible to help tank the tower shots and also help you deal damage to the enemy.

tip: When the enemy has been forced back to base after a fight or death, fast push the wave into their tower to apply pressure and set it up favorably for when you return to lane.
rationale: An empty enemy lane is the safest window to push hard without risking a response.
source_excerpt: You should fast push the wave so it pushes to the enemies tower. Doing this will allow you to deal damage to the enemy tower and apply pressure to it. Also, letting the wave bounce will leave it in a good place for when you finally come back to lane after Recalling.

tip: If your wave is too big to fully push under tower in time — due to a long death timer, enemy Teleport, or your own poor wave clear — thin it down instead, leaving a few ranged minions to slow push toward you.
rationale: Forcing a full fast push you can't actually execute in time wastes the window; converting to a slow push salvages the situation.
source_excerpt: You should make the wave slow push towards you. To do this, thin the wave down, kill all the enemy melee champions, and leave a few enemy ranged minions and then Recall.

tip: Before committing to a fast push, check whether you have time to do it, whether you can push quickly enough, and whether the wave is too big — if any answer is unfavorable, slow push instead.
rationale: This checklist decides whether a fast push will actually land in time or whether it's the wrong tool for the current wave size.
source_excerpt: Before you think about pushing the wave in this situation, think about these things: Do I have time to push? Can I push quick enough? Is the wave too big?

tip: If the enemy leaves lane to roam or teleport elsewhere, immediately start fast pushing your wave to punish their absence.
rationale: An empty lane is the ideal window to apply pressure without any risk of a response.
source_excerpt: If the enemy has gone to roam, or has Teleported to another lane, you should immediately start to fast push the wave.

tip: Before committing to a fast push when the enemy appears to leave lane, wait a few seconds to confirm they aren't baiting you.
rationale: Pushing in reaction to a fake absence can walk you straight into a trade you didn't need to take.
source_excerpt: Before choosing to fast push, leave it for a few seconds to make sure they’re not baiting you.

tip: After starting a fast push when the enemy leaves lane, choose between continuing to push for the tower or following the enemy to even a trade elsewhere — following is riskier since you may not catch them.
rationale: Each option trades a guaranteed local gain (tower pressure) against a less certain but potentially bigger one (map trade).
source_excerpt: Alternatively, you can follow the enemy as the soon as you’ve started the fast push. This can be good as you can make any trade even but is also quite dangerous as you may not be able to follow the enemy when they leave your lane.

tip: If you want to back but still want the wave to fast push while you're gone, leave 3 minions alive and then fully clear the next reinforcement wave before leaving — best done when you're ahead or the enemy is out of lane.
rationale: Clearing two waves' worth of minions in one pass builds a large fast-pushing wave that keeps working even after you've left.
source_excerpt: If you are wanting to back but also want the wave fast push quicker, you can leave the 3 minions alive, and then proceed to walk up to the next reinforcement wave and completely destroy all the minions. This is best done when you’re ahead of the enemy or when the enemy is either dead or out of lane and nobody is able to contest you.

tip: In top lane, fast push the wave before making a Teleport play or helping another lane, since it forces the enemy laner to either miss CS staying in lane or lose the ability to contest your play.
rationale: A fast-pushed wave puts the enemy top laner in a lose-lose between farming and reacting to your Teleport.
source_excerpt: When trying to make a Teleport play or when you’re trying to help another lane out, you need to apply a fast push to the lane.

tip: In top lane, if you want to take Rift Herald with your jungler, set up a slow push first so your lane keeps progressing rather than sitting frozen and exposing your tower while you're gone.
rationale: A frozen wave left unattended during a Herald play gives the enemy free pressure on your tower.
source_excerpt: If you want to take the Rift Herald with your Jungler, you should set up a slow push. This will allow your lane to be pushing and doing something while you’re gone.

tip: As jungler, don't waste time trying to gank a lane that's pushed up against your ally — unless you can dive, spend that time farming or taking other objectives instead.
rationale: A pushed lane removes the space needed to land a gank, so forcing it there wastes jungle time better spent elsewhere.
source_excerpt: Unless you can dive the enemy, you may be unable to gank any lane that is pushed up. Instead of wasting your time, you should spend it farming or looking to take other objectives.

tip: As jungler, look to gank lanes where the wave is even or frozen, since those wave states make a gank far easier to land.
rationale: An even or frozen wave gives the jungler room to approach and engage without the lane already being lost to overextension either way.
source_excerpt: If a lane is even, you may be able to gank it and if your allies are freezing, you will also be able to gank them.

tip: As jungler, when ganking an ally who's pushed under their own tower, expect only to relieve pressure rather than get a kill, since your laner likely can't follow up from that position.
rationale: A pushed-under-tower ally is defensively positioned, which limits what a gank there can realistically accomplish.
source_excerpt: You will probably be unable to kill the enemy unless you can 1v1 them because your laners may be unable to follow up. Try to relieve pressure, and do not expect to get the kill – so don’t flame them if they can’t follow up!

tip: As jungler, after a successful gank, help push the wave and pressure the tower, since taking the first tower early is often more valuable than most early drakes.
rationale: A gank's value compounds when it's converted into structural damage rather than just a kill.
source_excerpt: After a successful gank, you should help push the wave and apply pressure to the tower. Depending on the length of the enemies death time, you may be able to take the tower. A tower in the early game is more important than most drakes, so try and get the first tower when you can.

tip: As jungler, push the wave for your laner after a gank unless they've specifically asked you not to, since ignoring their preference can ruin their preferred lane state.
rationale: The laner has to live with the resulting wave state, so their stated preference should override the jungler's default instinct to push.
source_excerpt: With that said, if your ally doesn’t want the lane to be pushed- do not push it. It may ruin their laning experience and might make them mad. Unless they specify not to push, push the wave if you can.

tip: In mid lane, shove the wave in before going to help another lane, so it doesn't push back into your own tower while you're gone.
rationale: Mid lane's short length means an unattended wave crashes into your tower quickly if it isn't pushing away from it first.
source_excerpt: Before going to help any lanes out, you need to shove in the minion wave. Like the top lane with TP plays, you need the lane to be pushing so it doesn’t push against you while you’re gone.

tip: In mid lane, if the enemy has a champion notorious for level 2 ganks, don't push or overextend, since they'll punish it and keep camping you once they know you're vulnerable.
rationale: Provoking an early gank from a champion built around it invites a repeat problem rather than a one-off.
source_excerpt: If the enemy team has a champion who is notorious for level 2 ganks, be prepared for it. Do not push or overextend as they will gank and continue to camp you if they know you’re behind.

tip: In mid lane, default to keeping the wave closer to your own side rather than the enemy's, since mid is the easiest lane to gank and snowball.
rationale: Mid's dual jungle-entrance exposure makes a self-favoring wave position the safer baseline choice.
source_excerpt: Because the mid lane is arguably the easiest to gank and snowball, most of the time you will want the wave to be closer to your side of the lane rather than the enemies.

tip: When playing a mid lane champion who shoves the wave in early, keep strong map awareness and ward coverage to avoid cheeky ganks while pushed up.
rationale: A pushed-up wave removes your minion buffer against ganks, so vision has to compensate for the lost safety.
source_excerpt: When playing as a champion who shoves in early, have good map awareness and ward coverage to prevent any cheeky ganks from the enemy.

tip: At champion select, pick a bot lane duo with compatible wave-management styles, since pairing a hard-engage support with a champion who wants to push under tower makes the support relatively useless early.
rationale: Mismatched wave-state preferences between the ADC and support create an internal conflict the lane can never resolve.
source_excerpt: At champ select, try to choose a lane where you have good synergy between the ADC and Support. In a lane with little to no synergy, you will find yourself struggling to control waves as efficiently. For example, if you have a Support who needs to hard engage, you should not be playing somebody who wants to push the enemy under tower as it will make them relatively useless in the early stages of the game.

tip: As ADC, if your support dies, don't push the wave — let it come to you and freeze it outside your tower so your support can recover the XP and CS they missed.
rationale: A frozen wave lets a dead support catch back up on farm once they respawn instead of falling further behind.
source_excerpt: If your Support dies, try not to push the wave. Instead, let it come towards you and try to freeze it outside of your tower. Letting the wave freeze near your tower will allow your Support to pick up XP and CS that he missed.

tip: As ADC, when behind in a rough laning phase, keep the wave frozen on your side near your tier 2 tower and avoid pushing at all costs, so you can catch back up in farm.
rationale: Pushing while behind only hands the enemy more opportunities to deny and zone you further.
source_excerpt: When behind and having an unlucky laning phase, you will need to catch up in farm. To do this, keep the wave frozen on your side of the map near your tier 2 tower. Avoid pushing at all costs because you will get denied and not be able to catch up.

tip: As support, when your ADC wants to freeze near their tower, hold the wave outside your tower's range until the next minion wave arrives, so it doesn't get pushed under tower and reset.
rationale: The support's job in this state is to physically hold the wave in place while the ADC farms it down.
source_excerpt: If the ADC wants to freeze near their tower, your job as the Support is to hold the wave outside of the range so it doesn’t get pushed under your tower and reset. You need to hold it until the next minion wave comes.

tip: As support, help execute whatever wave state your ADC wants — thin it down, reset it, push it, or back — by continuing to auto attack and use your abilities to assist.
rationale: The ADC generally dictates lane state, so the support's role is to actively enable whichever plan they've chosen.
source_excerpt: Alternatively, if the ADC wants to thin it down, you should help and if they want it to reset- you need to also help them. If the ADC wants to back and Recall or he wants to push the wave, you need to also help him do that.

tip: As support, before roaming to help another lane, make sure your ADC will be safe and won't die while you're gone.
rationale: Leaving your ADC exposed in bot lane can turn a helpful roam into a losing trade for your own lane.
source_excerpt: Before you roam to help other lanes, make sure your ADC is going to be safe and not get killed while you’re gone.

tip: As support, if the lane is even rather than ahead, default to helping freeze the wave outside your ADC's tower, since pushing would let the enemy deny your ADC's farm.
rationale: An even lane state favors the safer default of freezing over the riskier option of pushing.
source_excerpt: In most situations, if you’re not ahead but are even, he will want it froze outside of his tower. If you push the wave, the enemy will be able to deny your ADC which will put him behind as he won’t be able to farm.

tip: When leashing for your jungler, leave lane by 1:37 or 1:38 at the latest so you don't miss lane minions and fall behind on experience.
rationale: Missing early lane minions can cost you the race to level 2 and 3 against your opponent.
source_excerpt: You should aim to leave no later than 1:37/1:38. If you leave later, you may miss out on some of the minions which will give the enemy the experience advantage over yourself which can allow them to hit level 2 and level 3 before you.

tip: If your jungler invaded and stole an enemy buff, leave the leash by 1:33 at the latest, since you still need to get back to your own lane to avoid falling behind.
rationale: A successful invade is only worth it if you don't sacrifice your own laning phase to help secure it.
source_excerpt: If you’ve invaded and stolen one of the enemies buffs, you will need to leave slightly earlier in order for you to not miss out anything. The latest you should leave is 1:33.

tip: Whenever you gain a level advantage over the enemy laner, be ready to engage or position to threaten them, since that's when your kit outclasses theirs.
rationale: A level lead is a temporary window of ability and stat advantage that's wasted if you don't use it to pressure the enemy.
source_excerpt: Whenever you hit a level advantage over the enemy, you should be prepared to engage on them or at the very least, put yourself in a position where you might be able to attack them.

tip: Study your specific champion's level power spikes so you know when you're strong and can play around your strengths rather than your weaknesses.
rationale: Knowing your own spike timings lets you deliberately choose when to be aggressive versus when to play safe.
source_excerpt: Every champion also has level power spikes, and each is different for many champions, but researching and having good knowledge on your champions logistics and dynamics will allow you to know when they are strong and when they are weak.

tip: Only attempt to zone an enemy champion off the wave if you have the advantage or the ability to out-trade them; without it you can't effectively zone them.
rationale: Zoning requires the threat of a winning fight to actually deter the enemy from farming.
source_excerpt: When you try to zone an enemy champion, you need to keep a few things in mind. Firstly, you must have the advantage or the ability to out-trade them if they decide to fight you. If you do not have this advantage, you can’t really zone them.

tip: When zoning an enemy champion, maintain good ward coverage so you don't get caught out while overextended.
rationale: Zoning inherently puts you forward of your normal position, so vision is what prevents that from becoming a liability.
source_excerpt: Secondly, you need to have good ward coverage so you do not get caught out while you’re overextended.

tip: You can pull the wave toward the enemy's side at level 1 by walking into lane early, setting the wave up to push toward you on the following waves and helping set up early jungler ganks.
rationale: Manipulating the very first wave state compounds into a favorable position for the next several waves.
source_excerpt: You may have seen a level 1 pull in some of your games where one player goes into lane early and pulls the wave slightly towards the enemies side of the lane. This allows the minions to be slightly further up in the lane. The technique is good to manipulate the wave and have it start of pushing towards you on the following waves.

tip: To keep a wave pushing on its own while you're away from lane, maintain at least a 4-minion advantage over the enemy in that lane.
rationale: An even wave naturally starts slow-pushing toward whichever side has more minions once it passes the halfway point, so a clear numbers edge is what sustains the push unattended.
source_excerpt: If you don’t want this to happen, make sure that you always have a 4 minion advantag e over the enemy in lane so it will keep pushing while you’re gone.

tip: Always maintain good ward coverage whenever you're pushing, freezing, or using any other wave management technique, since doing so without vision is highly risky.
rationale: Every wave management technique requires you to commit position and attention to the wave, which is exactly when you're most vulnerable without vision.
source_excerpt: Pushing, freezing and trying to deny or zone the enemy is done at great risk without proper ward coverage. Make sure that you have wards around your lane and around the map when you try to use wave control techniques.

tip: The number of bonus enemy minions in a frozen wave roughly equals the number of waves worth of farm you can deny them, so a well-held freeze compounds significantly.
rationale: Each extra minion held in the freeze represents an additional wave the enemy never gets to fully collect.
source_excerpt: The number of bonus enemy minions in a wave is the number of waves you can successfully freeze for. If there are 5 bonus minions in a wave, you could potentially deny the enemy at least 35 minions from the enemy.

tip: A wave will typically bounce off the tower the first time you push it under; only killing and pushing it again after that bounce will make it fully reset.
rationale: The tower doesn't clear a full pushed wave in one pass, so a second push is usually needed to force the reset state.
source_excerpt: Pro Tip: A wave will usually bounce off a tower first time around, if you kill and push the wave after it bounces, it will then reset.

tip: When trimming a wave down, prioritize killing the cannon minion first, since it both prevents the wave from pushing and reduces the damage it deals.
rationale: The cannon minion contributes disproportionately to both push power and wave damage, so removing it first has the biggest effect.
source_excerpt: Pro Tip: When trimming down a wave, make sure to take the cannon minion. This will prevent the wave from pushing if you want to freeze, and it will also prevent the wave from taking to much damage.

tip: To pull the wave, stay out of lane so the minions target you, then walk them into the river or a bush to keep them off your tower, dropping the pull once your reinforcements arrive.
rationale: Making yourself the minions' focus lets you physically relocate the wave to a safer spot than where it would otherwise crash.
source_excerpt: Pull the wave: Pulling the wave is where you have no minions in lane and you make the minions focus you. While they are focusing you, you can start walking into them and around the lane to prevent them from walking under your tower and killing themselves. You will usually pull a wave into the start of the river, or into the bushes.

tip: When pulling the wave, don't hold it for too long, since you'll take significant damage from the minions — thin it down first if you're unable to tank it.
rationale: Pulling trades your own health for wave position, so the technique only stays worthwhile for a limited window.
source_excerpt: Pro Tip: When pulling a wave, you may have to thin it down and kill a few of the minions if you’re unable to tank them. Make sure that you do not pull the wave for too long as you will take a lot of damage from the minions.

tip: As a brand-new player, start with League's in-game tutorial before jumping into real matches.
rationale: It's the fastest way to get comfortable with basic movement, abilities, and item purchases before facing real opponents.
source_excerpt: First up, the best place for any new player to start is the League tutorial.

tip: Pick Flash as one of your two summoner spells in almost every game once you've unlocked it.
rationale: Its short-cooldown escape and engage utility make it valuable in nearly every matchup, which is why it's the default second summoner spell.
source_excerpt: I say pick, but basically one of those is almost always going to be flash once you unlock it

tip: As a beginner, put your skill point into whichever ability is highlighted when you level up.
rationale: The game's recommended ability highlight reflects a sensible default skill order, so following it saves a new player from having to learn ability priority from scratch.
source_excerpt: recommended ability is just going to start flashing when you gain a level, and you can confidently put your point there as a beginner.

tip: As a new player, hide the character/rune stats panel to reduce screen clutter.
rationale: That information isn't actionable for a beginner yet, so keeping it hidden simplifies the HUD and keeps focus on the essentials.
source_excerpt: we're going to recommend just hiding it for now and reduce the screen clutter and just keep things really, really simple.

tip: Check the minimap in quick glances during downtime, like when walking back to lane, rather than trying to watch it constantly.
rationale: Trying to track everything on the map at once is overwhelming for a beginner, and awareness improves naturally with quick, well-timed glances.
source_excerpt: glances during the downtime that you have, like when you're walking back to lane or when nothing urgent is going to be happening on your screen.

tip: As a beginner, don't stress about tracking every objective timer -- that awareness comes naturally with experience.
rationale: Objective knowledge is something that builds up through repeated play, so worrying about it early just adds unnecessary pressure.
source_excerpt: And when just starting out, please do not stress too much about objectives.

tip: Don't leave your lane to roam for kills without good reason -- you bleed gold and experience from minions the whole time you're gone.
rationale: Missed minions cost steady, guaranteed gold and experience, so an opportunistic roam has to be worth more than that loss.
source_excerpt: Sure, you might pick up a kill or two roaming around the map to other lanes, but you'd be bleeding gold and bleeding experience the entire time you do it.

tip: Prioritize last-hitting minions -- it's one of the most crucial skills to develop to get better at League.
rationale: Consistent last hits are a steady, low-risk source of gold and experience that compounds over the course of a lane.
source_excerpt: that last hit on minions is one of the most crucial skills to develop in League and get better.

tip: Value winning a trade even without a kill, since forcing your opponent to recall denies them gold and experience while they're away.
rationale: A recall costs the opponent an entire minion wave's worth of gold and experience, which is a real gain even without a kill.
source_excerpt: You could force that champion to have to return to base and heal. They're going to miss out on gold and experience from minions while they're gone.

tip: When you have lane priority, use it to leave your lane first and help your team contest objectives.
rationale: Lane priority means your opponent can't punish your lane while you're gone, so it's the safe window to go help elsewhere.
source_excerpt: happens, you've now got what we like to call lane priority. Just a fancy way of saying that you're the one in control. With lane priority, you're able to leave your lane first if your team needs help

tip: As a beginner, trust the game's suggested rune pages and recommended item builds.
rationale: Those suggestions are pulled from what other players commonly build on that champion, so they're a safe, low-effort starting point.
source_excerpt: you honestly really can't go wrong here as all Riot does is pull the data for these items and rune builds from what other players are most commonly building on that specific champion.

tip: Switch your camera setting from dynamic to free camera.
rationale: Dynamic camera restricts your view and makes it harder to track fights, which is why experienced players use free camera instead.
source_excerpt: the majority of players opt for free camera as this just gives you complete control.

tip: Reduce your HUD size from the default 100 down to around 50.
rationale: A smaller HUD leaves more of your screen visible for tracking the actual game.
source_excerpt: reduce the size of the HUD. By default, this is set to 100, but we recommend somewhere around 50

tip: Increase the size of your minimap from its default setting.
rationale: A larger minimap makes it easier to read at a glance, which directly improves map awareness.
source_excerpt: we suggest increasing the size of your mini map.

tip: Enable the 'show spell cost' setting so ability mana costs display on their icons.
rationale: Seeing mana costs at a glance makes it easy to tell whether you can afford your full combo before committing to a fight.
source_excerpt: enable show spell cost, which is located right here.

tip: If you want a support who heals, shields, and buffs to keep allies safe, play Milio as a beginner.
rationale: His whole kit is built around protecting and empowering allies, making the enchanter playstyle intuitive to pick up.
source_excerpt: If you're looking to heal, shield, buff, and keep your allies safe, then Milio does it all.

tip: If you want a tanky, engage-focused support who creates plays by locking enemies down, play Leona as a beginner.
rationale: Her kit is built entirely around chaining crowd control to lock down a target, making the engage playstyle straightforward to learn.
source_excerpt: But if rather than keeping your team alive, you enjoy making plays, being a tanky frontliner, and locking enemies down, you need to try out Leona.

tip: To find a champion you enjoy, browse the collections tab, click on one that looks interesting, and read what its abilities do.
rationale: Trying out champions by their abilities is a low-commitment way for a beginner to discover a playstyle they like.
source_excerpt: Takes time to learn, but if you want to know which one to play, just go to the collections tab, go to champions, click one you think looks cool, and click abilities and read what they do.

tip: If you don't recognize an enemy champion in game, mouse over their name in the scoreboard to find it, then look them up on the league wiki.
rationale: Knowing what an unfamiliar enemy's kit does is necessary to play around their threats, and this is the fastest way to learn it mid-game.
source_excerpt: mouse over their name in the scoreboard, find their champion name, and look it up on the league wiki.

tip: To learn how to build a champion, read its abilities to see what stats they scale with, then build items around those stats.
rationale: A champion's scaling stats determine which items actually make its abilities stronger, so reading the kit text is the direct way to figure out a build.
source_excerpt: So, if you want to learn your character, read the abilities and then read what they scale with, and then that'll tell you what items to build.

tip: As a beginner, just buy the game's recommended items rather than trying to memorize the full item pool.
rationale: The suggested shop items are a reasonable default build, so leaning on them lets a new player play instead of getting stuck memorizing 200+ items.
source_excerpt: memorize over 200 items and all the stats and unique passives they have, but I'll make it easy for you. Just buy the recommended items.

tip: Weigh champion pick before committing to a roaming gameplan — some champions (e.g. Alistar) roam far more effectively than others (e.g. Janna).
rationale: A champion's kit determines whether a roam is likely to succeed, so roam frequency should scale with the champion you're playing.
source_excerpt: Every champion and role can roam, but some will find more success than others. For example, Janna will find it hard to roam; whereas Alistar would thrive.

tip: Do most of your roaming in the early-to-mid game, especially during laning phase.
rationale: Enemies are more likely to be isolated or in smaller numbers during laning phase, making kills or objectives easier to secure.
source_excerpt: Roaming is usually done during the early to mid stages of the game, especially during the laning phase. This is because the likelihood of gaining a kill or achieving your goal is far more probable since enemies will be more likely to be in isolation or fewer numbers.

tip: Treat roaming as a necessity rather than an optional play, given how much tower plating has extended the laning phase.
rationale: A longer laning phase means more time and more opportunity windows for roams to pay off before towers fall on their own.
source_excerpt: Because of this extension to the early game, roaming is now a necessity rather than something you might do.

tip: Roam to a lane if an ally there is struggling and falling behind in levels, experience, or gold.
rationale: Forcing the enemy to recall or killing them can pull a struggling ally back into the game before the gap becomes unrecoverable.
source_excerpt: This is why it is important that you look to roam if any ally is struggling and falling behind in levels, experience or gold.

tip: Roam to punish enemies who have built up a large bounty.
rationale: A large shutdown bounty converts a single kill into an outsized gold swing for your team.
source_excerpt: You may want to roam during this time as you’ll be able to gain the shut down from the enemy.

tip: After a successful roam kill, pressure the enemy's tower and gold plates while the lane is open.
rationale: Taking plates or a tower off the back of a roam opens up the map and makes future roams easier.
source_excerpt: After successfully roaming to a lane, you may be able to apply pressure to the enemy’s tower and their gold plates.

tip: If a lane keeps overextending for farm after your first gank, keep roaming back to punish it repeatedly.
rationale: Repeated roams to a lane that must overextend for CS can snowball into several kills instead of just one.
source_excerpt: You may also be able to continuously gank a lane and put the enemy behind if they have to overextend for farm.

tip: Only roam when you have a clear intention and stand to gain something from it.
rationale: Roaming without a purpose wastes time you could have spent farming or defending your own lane.
source_excerpt: When roaming to another lane, always keep your intentions in mind and make sure to only roam if you can get something out of it.

tip: Don't chase an arbitrary roam-count goal — roam as often as good opportunities present themselves instead.
rationale: Following a fixed timer or number ignores whether the actual game state makes a roam worthwhile.
source_excerpt: Instead, you should aim to roam as often as you can if you have the opportunity to do so.

tip: Roam directly from base rather than from your lane when you can.
rationale: Leaving lane is visible to the enemy and lets them call it out and back off; roaming from base hides your whereabouts.
source_excerpt: Roaming from your base can bring a surprise element to roaming. As the enemy will not see you leave your lane, they may not expect you to be there.

tip: Prefer roaming from base when possible, since it lets you switch directions and return to lane if the roam isn't panning out en route.
rationale: Committing from your own lane forecloses that flexibility once you're already gone.
source_excerpt: Roaming from base will allow you to switch directions and return to your lane if things do not seem to be working out en route.

tip: When roaming from base, keep an eye on your own lane and be ready to return immediately if the enemy arrives there before you and starts pushing.
rationale: An unattended lane can be pushed into your tower while you're committed to a roam elsewhere.
source_excerpt: If the enemy gets to lane before you, they may start pushing the wave which means you’ll need to return as soon as you can.

tip: If you notice the enemy moving toward a particular lane, rotate there to counter-gank their attempt.
rationale: Meeting the enemy's gank with your own numbers advantage turns their play into a losing one.
source_excerpt: If you notice that the enemy is looking to move towards one lane in particular, you can try and counter their gank.

tip: If you spot the enemy jungler moving through the river toward a gank, head to that lane to counter-gank them as well.
rationale: Arriving alongside your laner flips a planned enemy gank into a losing fight for them.
source_excerpt: Alternatively, if you notice that the enemy Jungler is moving through the river in order to gank, you could head towards the lane as well to counter gank them.

tip: As Support, roam when your ADC can hold their own in lane for a while, such as on Ezreal or Draven.
rationale: A self-sufficient ADC lets you apply pressure elsewhere without risking their lane state.
source_excerpt: If your ADC is somebody who can play independently for a brief period of time, roaming when they’re in lane alone is a good way of applying pressure.

tip: Avoid roaming as Support if your ADC is behind or has no way to escape.
rationale: Leaving a vulnerable ADC alone in lane risks losing them for a roam that may not even pay off.
source_excerpt: If your ADC is behind or has no possibility to escape, roaming while they’re in lane can be difficult.

tip: While roaming as Support, keep checking on your lane and how your ADC is faring — return as soon as they start to struggle.
rationale: Their safety takes priority over completing a roam that's no longer safe to finish.
source_excerpt: While gone, keep an eye on your lane and how your ADC is fairing up. If they seem to be struggling, return as soon as you can.

tip: If your ADC can't be left alone safely, wait until they've backed before roaming.
rationale: Once your ADC is out of lane they can't be put at risk by your absence, making it the safest roam window.
source_excerpt: If your ADC is somebody of the insecure type and is unable to farm while you’re gone, your best bet is to roam when they’ve backed.

tip: As Support, only roam when your ADC can't be put behind by your absence.
rationale: Your ADC's safety and resource gain should never be the cost of your roam.
source_excerpt: One of the biggest things to remember when roaming is that your ADC should not be put behind by your roam, so roaming when they can’t be put behind is key.

tip: Once your ADC is out of lane, move quickly to roam, get the play, and head back to base before they return.
rationale: Speed maximizes the value you extract from the safe window your ADC's absence creates.
source_excerpt: Once they’re no longer in lane, you need to start moving as quickly as you can so you’re able to roam > gank > and head back to base.

tip: Set up a roam by backing before your ADC does, giving yourself breathing room to roam and return in time.
rationale: Backing early buys you extra free time compared to waiting for your ADC's own recall.
source_excerpt: It can allow you to set up a roam by backing before your ADC does. This will give you some breathing room to roam and return to lane.

tip: Prioritize roaming when your ultimate is up, especially on champions whose ults struggle to secure solo kills but shine on ganks.
rationale: Some kits convert far better into kills with a second body present than they do in a 1v1 lane exchange.
source_excerpt: This is why I recommend that you should look to roam if you have your ultimate up.

tip: Twisted Fate's ultimate is nearly worthless unless he's actively roaming with it, so prioritize roaming whenever it's up.
rationale: His ult's value comes almost entirely from map-wide gank potential rather than anything it does in his own lane.
source_excerpt: Twisted Fate’s ultimate, for example, is practically useless unless he is roaming.

tip: As Twisted Fate, keep an eye on the map for low-health enemies so you can use your roaming ultimate opportunistically nearby.
rationale: Watching health bars across the map lets you convert his global ult into a kill the moment an opening appears.
source_excerpt: Always keep an eye on the map to check what health players are sitting at. If somebody is low enough, try to use your ultimate nearby.

tip: Gank for an ally who's stuck in lane under pressure but has a strong crowd-control ultimate up.
rationale: Their CC ultimate has excellent follow-up potential that a gank lets them finally use.
source_excerpt: As his Ult is considered crowd control, and as he has great follow up potential in general, ganking him when he has his ultimate up is a no brainer.

tip: Prioritize ganking immobile allies with game-changing ultimates, such as Sion, Malphite, Nautilus, Ornn, or Rumble.
rationale: These champions can't roam to use their ultimates themselves, so a gank is often the only way they cash in their kit's power.
source_excerpt: Champions who fit these criteria are Sion , Malphite , Nautilus , Ornn or Rumble who all have good game changing ultimates, but sometimes are unable to do anything with them because they are immobile or unable to roam.

tip: After killing your enemy laner (or they've recalled), take the opportunity to roam while your lane is safe.
rationale: With the enemy off the map, there's no pressure on your own lane, which is a favorable condition for roaming.
source_excerpt: If the enemy laner has died – or for one reason or another(like recalling) is not in lane anymore, you should try to roam and do something while they’re not there.

tip: If you need to back after a play, recall rather than trying to squeeze in a roam first.
rationale: Skipping your own item and level spike to chase a roam can cost more than the roam gains.
source_excerpt: It is important to remember, however, if you need to back, you should recall and not roam.

tip: Time your return to lane to coincide with the enemy's respawn so you don't miss out on farm, XP, or lane pressure.
rationale: Coming back too late gives the enemy free CS and tempo in your absence.
source_excerpt: Also, keep an eye on your own lane and get back there at the same time as the enemy so you do not miss out on farm, XP or lane pressure.

tip: Roam to punish enemies who are missing a defensive Summoner Spell, and track spell usage across lanes to know when.
rationale: A defenseless enemy laner can't escape or peel, turning a normal gank into a near-guaranteed kill.
source_excerpt: If an enemy champion has no defense capability because they have used one of their Summoner Spells in a previous exchange, you can abuse the fact that they’re defenseless and pick up some free kills.

tip: Visit a lane frequently once you know its enemy laner has no Flash.
rationale: Without Flash their movement becomes predictable, letting you punish it repeatedly.
source_excerpt: I recommend visiting an ally frequently if their enemy laner has no Flash. Because their movement in lane can be relatively scripted, you should abuse the fact that they’re defenseless

tip: Ganking Annie when her Flash is down is likely to net a nearly free kill.
rationale: Annie is rather immobile, so removing her one escape tool makes her extremely vulnerable to a gank.
source_excerpt: For example, as Annie is rather immobile, ganking her when her Flash is down is likely to result in basically free kills.

tip: Expect lower roam success against an enemy who still has Flash up, since they can escape or dodge your crowd control.
rationale: A ready Flash is a get-out-of-jail-free card that neutralizes most gank attempts.
source_excerpt: When an enemy has their Flash, a reward through roaming can sometimes be difficult because they may be able to escape or dodge your crowd control.

tip: Follow the enemy roamer when they leave their lane rather than letting them create a numbers advantage elsewhere unopposed.
rationale: Matching their roam prevents them from turning their target lane into a favorable 2v1 or 3v2.
source_excerpt: This is why it is crucial that you try and follow the enemy laner if they’re roaming.

tip: If you're strong in 1v1s, like on Zed or Akali, directly follow the enemy roamer rather than taking a longer defensive route.
rationale: A confident duelist can afford to chase directly since they're favored if the fight comes down to a 1v1.
source_excerpt: In some cases, you will be able to directly follow the enemy if you’re good in a 1v1 setting. Champions such as Zed or Akali are really good in this situation.

tip: If you're behind or weak in 1v1s, take a defensive alternate route rather than directly following the enemy roamer.
rationale: A defensive path keeps you safe from ambush-prone assassins who wait for pursuers to walk past them.
source_excerpt: However, if you’re behind or not very good in a 1v1 environment, you will have to take an alternative route to get to another lane.

tip: Be wary of bait roams — don't rush to push the wave or chase the enemy the instant they seem to be leaving.
rationale: A few seconds late is a far better outcome than walking straight into a trap.
source_excerpt: Many champions like to bait roams. So, keep this in mind and do not push the wave straight away or directly follow the enemy as you may be falling into a trap.

tip: If you can't follow the enemy's roam, push your own wave to threaten their tower and force them back to defend.
rationale: Applying pressure to their tower gives them a reason to abandon the roam and return.
source_excerpt: If you cannot follow the enemy, push the wave and draw them back to your lane by applying pressure to the tower.

tip: Join your jungler on their gank whenever you can rather than staying in lane.
rationale: Turning a 2v1 into a 3v1 or 4v2 puts the odds heavily in your favor.
source_excerpt: Making any exchange 3v1 or 4v2 puts the odds highly in your favor.

tip: As a Support with weak solo roaming potential, like Janna, pair up with your jungler to roam effectively together.
rationale: Going with a jungler compensates for a kit that struggles to force plays on its own.
source_excerpt: When you’re playing as a Support that lacks roaming potential, going with your Jungler increases your stature and roaming capability.

tip: Prioritize minimizing collateral damage while roaming rather than expecting a perfect outcome.
rationale: A few missed minions are a small price compared to a gold lead or a tower.
source_excerpt: As no game is perfect, you should prioritize minimizing the collateral damage when you’re gone. For example, a few minions missed is nothing compared to a gold lead and a possible tower.

tip: Recognize that champions without hard CC or high damage, like Janna, Soraka, Lulu, or Nasus, struggle to force successful roams.
rationale: Roams succeed on the back of crowd control or damage; without either, the enemy can usually just walk away.
source_excerpt: Champions that are great at roaming are ones that have either high amounts of damage or crowd control.

tip: Champions like Alistar, Lissandra, Thresh, Pyke, and Twisted Fate are especially strong roamers thanks to kits built around it.
rationale: Their kits are specifically designed to enable ganks, so roaming plays directly to their strengths.
source_excerpt: Alistar , Lissandra , Thresh , Pyke and Twisted Fate are all fantastic at roaming because their kit supplements it.

tip: If you're not playing a champion designed to roam, don't over-invest in roaming at the expense of your own scaling.
rationale: Forcing roams on a champion whose kit doesn't support it hurts your own development for limited payoff.
source_excerpt: As a side note, if you aren’t roaming with a champion designed to do so, you ARE hurting yourself.

tip: Weigh that Twisted Fate's ultimate loses relative value in late-game 5v5 teamfights compared to a scaling mid laner like Orianna.
rationale: A roam-focused ultimate matters less once the game shifts to coordinated teamfights around objectives like Baron.
source_excerpt: For example, once late game arrives, TF’s ultimate is much less useful in a 5v5 teamfight at Baron in comparison to another Mid laner, such as Orianna.

tip: Check the state of your target lane before committing to leave your own lane.
rationale: Roaming without checking risks wasting time on a lane that isn't actually gankable.
source_excerpt: Checking out how your other lanes are doing is a must before you set up and leave your own lane.

tip: Don't roam to a lane whose wave is pushed into the enemy tower unless you're able to dive.
rationale: The enemy is already safe under their tower, so there's no play to make without a dive.
source_excerpt: If a lane is pushing for example, unless you can dive the enemy, there is no point going to gank them because you will not be able to do anything as the enemy is already under their tower.

tip: Check both your ally's and the enemy's health before committing to a gank — if either is very low, it may not be worth the trip.
rationale: A low-health player on either side is likely to just back off rather than fight, wasting the roam.
source_excerpt: Another thing to look out for is the health of your ally and the enemy. If either one of them is rather low, it may be non-beneficial to gank or roam because either one of them will have to back off.

tip: A wave pushed into the enemy tower will eventually bounce back toward the middle of the lane — that reset moment is a good ganking opportunity.
rationale: The bounce briefly puts the wave in a neutral position where a gank is more likely to land.
source_excerpt: If the wave is being pushed into the enemy’s tower, it will bounce or reset eventually. This can leave it in the middle of the lane which can give you a good chance at ganking.

tip: Avoid roaming to gank a lane where the enemy is freezing on their side, unless you can dive or your ally can push the wave to bounce it.
rationale: A frozen wave on the enemy's side gives you no safe approach angle for a gank.
source_excerpt: Generally, avoid roaming if the enemy if freezing on their side of the lane. Unless you can dive or your ally can push and make it bounce.

tip: It's a good time to roam to a lane where the wave is pushed into your ally's tower or your ally is freezing.
rationale: Either state gives you a safe angle to approach and set up the gank.
source_excerpt: If the wave is being pushed into your ally’s tower, or they are freezing, it can be a good time to roam.

tip: If the wave you're roaming toward is stacking up, ask your ally to trim it down before you arrive.
rationale: A stacked wave keeps your ally tied down last-hitting instead of being free to help you fight.
source_excerpt: However, if the wave is stacking, they will be unable to help you once you go in, so ask them to trim it down prior to your arrival.

tip: Before roaming to gank, check that your ally has their ultimate up and enough health to follow up once you engage.
rationale: Their follow-up damage and CC materially raise your odds of actually securing the kill.
source_excerpt: While not necessary, if your ally has their ultimate up, it would be easier for your team to secure the kill.

tip: Avoid ganking for a low-mana ally unless you can supply the damage yourself, such as on Morgana or Pyke.
rationale: Without mana they may be unable to follow up with abilities, making the gank a wasted trip unless you can carry it.
source_excerpt: If your ally doesn’t have much mana, they may be unable to follow up with damage through their auto attacks. This would be a wasteful time to gank unless you have enough damage, like Morgana or Pyke .

tip: As Support, confirm your ADC can farm, stay alive, and avoid being denied before you commit to a roam.
rationale: The ADC's safety is the Support's main priority, and roaming shouldn't come at the cost of it.
source_excerpt: The Supports main priority should be the ADC’s life and they should still be able to: farm, stay alive and not get denied.

tip: Ezreal is a good candidate to leave alone while roaming, since his Q and E let him farm safely for a short period.
rationale: His kit gives him poke and escape that most ADCs lack, letting him hold his own without Support presence.
source_excerpt: Ezreal, for example, is a great laner that can safely play alone for a small period of time thanks to his Q and his E.

tip: Avoid roaming as Support if your ADC is immobile and squishy, like Kog'Maw.
rationale: An ADC with no escape and low durability can't be safely left alone in lane.
source_excerpt: However, if your ADC is somebody like a Kog’Maw who is rather immobile and squishy- you should not roam.

tip: For defenseless, no-escape ADCs like Kog'Maw, Jhin, or Twitch, don't roam while they're still in lane — wait until they're guaranteed safe, or roam from base instead.
rationale: These ADCs have no way to disengage if caught, so leaving them in lane while you're gone is high-risk.
source_excerpt: If your ADC is somebody who cannot be left alone because they’re either defenseless or have no escape ability like Kog , Jhin , Twitch then you should not roam when they’re in lane.

tip: Push your wave before leaving lane rather than abandoning it outright.
rationale: An uncontested wave lets the enemy push straight into your tower and start dealing damage while you're gone.
source_excerpt: If you were to just drop everything and leave lane, the enemy would be able to push the wave almost instantly into your tower and start dealing damage to it.

tip: Push the wave into the enemy tower before roaming to create a buffer that works in your favor.
rationale: The enemy has to spend time clearing that wave, which delays any attempt to punish your empty lane.
source_excerpt: This is why you need to make sure that you push the wave before leaving. Directly pushing it will cause a buffer effect that works in your favor.

tip: Pushing a larger wave into the enemy tower before roaming buys you more time away, since it takes longer to clear without much AOE damage.
rationale: A bigger wave is a bigger time cost for the enemy to clean up before they can punish your empty lane.
source_excerpt: If the wave that you’ve pushed into the enemies tower is rather large, it will give you more time to roam and it will take the enemy longer to clear it if they do not have much damage or AOE abilities.

tip: Communicate your roaming intentions to your team before leaving lane or base.
rationale: Your teammates can only prepare for and capitalize on your roam if they know it's coming.
source_excerpt: Before leaving your lane or moving from base, make sure that you communicate with your team and tell them your intentions.

tip: Spam the 'on my way' ping repeatedly while roaming so your ally doesn't miss it.
rationale: A single ping is easy to miss mid-fight, so repeating it ensures your ally actually notices.
source_excerpt: Typically, you would use the “on my way” ping and use it repetitively while you’re on your way. I recommend that you borderline spam it to ensure that your allies take notice.

tip: Use directional 'on my way' pings to lay out your specific route, not just your destination.
rationale: Telling your ally which path you're taking lets them time their own play around your exact arrival.
source_excerpt: You can also use the “OMW” ping to lay out a determined route for yourself.

tip: Take the most efficient route when roaming rather than a suboptimal one.
rationale: A slower path can make you arrive too late to help or secure the kill.
source_excerpt: Something that is heavily overlooked when roaming is the route that you take. If you take a suboptimal route, you may find that you get to the designated lane at a later time which may ruin your chances of helping your team or securing a kill.

tip: Review your replays to evaluate whether your roam pathing and timing were optimal.
rationale: Deliberate review is how roaming judgment and route efficiency actually improve over time.
source_excerpt: Be sure to watch your replays (which you should already be doing), to see if your pathing was optimal and how your timing could have been improved.

tip: As Support, roam from bot lane to mid through the river when possible.
rationale: It runs directly to mid and is usually the most time-efficient route with a high chance of success.
source_excerpt: In a lot of cases, this will be the route you’ll take as it is the most time efficient with a high chance of success.

tip: Take the defensive route through your own jungle instead of the river when you lack vision control.
rationale: Without vision, the river route exposes you to being caught by an unseen enemy.
source_excerpt: In most cases, especially if you don’t have a ton of vision control, you’ll only want to take a defensive route if you want to be safe.

tip: When matching an enemy Support's roam, take a defensive route rather than following them directly.
rationale: Following directly lets them simply turn around and collapse on you.
source_excerpt: For example, if you’re following the enemy Support and trying to match their roam, you would want to take a defensive route rather than follow them directly as they can just turn around and collapse on you.

tip: Take the jungle route instead of the river if the river is warded or the Scuttle Crab is already gone.
rationale: Both conditions mean the river offers no informational or objective advantage anymore.
source_excerpt: There are also some other reasons why you may want to take this route such as if you know that the Scuttle Crab has been taken or the river is warded.

tip: As Blue side, favor the defensive jungle route more often than the river.
rationale: Map geometry leaves Blue side more overextended when roaming through the river than Red side is.
source_excerpt: Due to the architecture of the map, the Blue team will be ‘more’ overextended going through the river- which is why it’s favored for you to sometimes take a more defensive route through your own jungle.

tip: As Red side, only roam through the enemy's jungle to dive or rotate mid under strict conditions, like when you're winning lane or have already killed the enemy bot laners.
rationale: Routing through the enemy's own jungle is inherently risky and only pays off when you already hold an advantage.
source_excerpt: We’ve avoided displaying this route as you should only take it in strict circumstances such as if you’re winning lane or you’ve killed the enemy bottom laners.

tip: As a top laner, only roam when you have a lane edge or a clear kill opportunity elsewhere.
rationale: Top roams are otherwise not worth the CS and tempo lost from leaving lane.
source_excerpt: Top laners generally do not roam unless they have an edge in the lane or they know that they can pick up a kill by roaming.

tip: Top laners with strong ganking ultimates, like Hecarim or Sion, can roam to mid, land their ult, and return to top.
rationale: Their ultimates convert well into a mid-lane gank even though they aren't native to that lane.
source_excerpt: For example, Hecarim could run to the mid lane and cast his ultimate on the enemy and then return back to the top lane: the same goes for Sion .

tip: Take the river route when roaming aggressively from top lane.
rationale: The river is the fastest way to press an advantage into mid lane.
source_excerpt: If you’re playing aggressively, you will always want to take the route through the river.

tip: If you're ahead as a top laner, take the deeper route into the enemy jungle when roaming.
rationale: Being stronger than the enemy gives you roaming priority even on a riskier path.
source_excerpt: Or if you’re ahead, you can take the deeper route into the enemy’s jungle. This is because you’re stronger than the enemy and should have roaming priority.

tip: As a top laner running Teleport, use it to open up ganking options beyond your normal roam routes.
rationale: Teleport lets you convert map awareness directly into a gank without physically walking there first.
source_excerpt: Top laners are also the most likely role to take Teleport. This opens many more ganking options and will reward players with better map and game sense.

tip: As Blue side top laner, don't roam if the enemy is pushing the wave toward you.
rationale: They'll be able to take your tower while you're away from lane.
source_excerpt: As the blue team, if the enemy is pushing the wave towards you, you’ll never want to roam as the enemy will be able to get your tower.

tip: Take the defensive jungle route from top to surprise-gank another lane, especially when the enemy top is freezing or denying your farm.
rationale: A defensive route both hides your approach and makes sense when your own lane offers little to do.
source_excerpt: This is also a good route to take if the enemy is freezing or denying you farm.

tip: Approach the mid lane from the side closest to the enemy laner's current position.
rationale: Attacking from the near side maximizes your chance of catching them before they can react.
source_excerpt: You need to look at where both the Mid laners are and attack from the side that is closest to the enemy.

tip: If the wave is in the middle of mid lane, approach from slightly behind the enemy to cut off their escape.
rationale: Coming from behind makes it harder for them to simply walk away from the gank.
source_excerpt: If the wave is in the middle of the lane, you should look at approach slightly from behind the enemy to cut them off and make it difficult for them to escape.

tip: Never approach a gank from the route closest to your own ally.
rationale: That route telegraphs the gank and ruins the element of surprise.
source_excerpt: You would never use the route closest to your ally as the element of surprise would be ruined.

tip: Before diving the enemy mid laner on a gank, communicate your intentions and confirm the wave is under the enemy's tower.
rationale: Without coordination the mid laner may not follow up, and without the wave state the dive itself may be unsafe.
source_excerpt: Before doing so, make sure that you’ve communicated to the Mid laner your intentions and make sure that the minion wave is under the enemy’s tower too.

tip: As a mid laner, use your central map position to roam to either side lane and snowball your lead across the map.
rationale: Mid's position lets you convert a winning lane into map-wide pressure much like a second jungler.
source_excerpt: With the potential to be anywhere and everywhere, much like a Jungler, they can solo win a game by winning their lane and snowballing their lead to help other lanes.

tip: Sometimes loop around the map on an indirect path when roaming from mid rather than always taking the most direct route.
rationale: A less obvious path can catch enemies off guard even at the cost of a few extra seconds.
source_excerpt: While it’s important to take the most efficient route when possible, in some cases you may benefit from looping around the map by not taking a direct path.

tip: Use the Blast Cone to escape or dodge wards when roaming through the blue tri-brush.
rationale: It gives you an alternate exit that avoids common ward placements in that area.
source_excerpt: You can also utilize the Blast Cone to escape and dodge any potential wards inside the blue tri-brush.

tip: Mobile champions with dashes or leaps, like LeBlanc using her W to cross walls, benefit heavily from taking non-direct roaming routes.
rationale: Their mobility tools let them cut through terrain that would slow down a champion without one.
source_excerpt: LeBlanc , for example, benefits heavily from this type of roaming technique as she can use your W to get over walls.

tip: As Support, always take a designated roaming route from base to lane rather than mindlessly walking straight to bot.
rationale: A designated route keeps a roam option alive the whole way, whereas walking straight bot forecloses it.
source_excerpt: This is why I recommend that whenever you’re playing as the Support, you always take one of these designated routes to lane rather than tabbing out and just mindlessly walking bot.

tip: A few top laners, like Sion, Camille, or Malphite, can also effectively roam directly from base, unlike most other top laners.
rationale: Their kits allow them to profitably detour from base the same way a Support typically does.
source_excerpt: More often than not, the only role that does this is the Support with the exception of a few Top laners such as Sion , Camille or Malphite .

tip: As Support, decide on your roam plan before heading to lane rather than waiting until you're already there.
rationale: Deciding late wastes the precious time and XP that an early decision would have preserved.
source_excerpt: If you were to walk bot and then decide that you want to roam, you would have wasted precious time and you may miss out on experience because of your negligence.

tip: While walking your base-to-lane route as Support, keep an eye on what's happening in mid lane and around the map.
rationale: That awareness is what lets you decide whether to divert into a roam along the way.
source_excerpt: As you walk through your own jungle, you should keep an eye on what is happening in the mid lane and around the map.

tip: Reassess at each map cross-section whether to continue toward a roam or return to your own lane.
rationale: The target lane's state can change mid-walk, so bail out if it stops looking gankable.
source_excerpt: If at any point the lane changes and doesn’t seem to be in a gankable position anymore, you can simply return to your own lane.

tip: Abort your roam and return to lane if your ally has taken heavy damage on the way there.
rationale: A badly hurt ally makes the gank a likely lost cause not worth continuing to pursue.
source_excerpt: If you see that your ally has taken a beating while you’re on your way, you may have to turn tail and head back to your own lane as the roam may be a lost cause.

tip: If your ally has just used their key damage or CC ability before you arrive, wait for it to come off cooldown before engaging the gank.
rationale: Engaging without their follow-up available reduces the odds of securing the kill.
source_excerpt: If your ally has just used their main source of damage or crowd control before you get there, you may have to wait for it to be up again before going in.

tip: Watch your own lane while roaming, and return promptly if the enemy laner starts racking up CS.
rationale: Letting the enemy farm unchecked in your absence quickly erodes any advantage the roam creates.
source_excerpt: If you notice that the enemy is starting to get a good amount of CS, return as soon as you can so you can to ensure you do not fall behind.

tip: Return to lane to protect your tower if the enemy starts pushing your wave back while you're roaming.
rationale: An unattended pushing wave puts your own tower at direct risk.
source_excerpt: If you notice that the enemy has started to push the wave back, you’ll need to return to lane and protect your tower.

tip: Avoid letting the enemy take a tower or destroy plating while you're roaming, unless you're securing an equal or better trade.
